topic.subject: science
topic.title: Control and coordination
topic.scope: neurons, reflex arc, brain, plant hormones and tropisms, animal hormones, feedback

misconceptions.statement: Nerve impulses travel across the synapse as electrical sparks.
misconceptions.why: Students often think of the nervous system as a continuous electrical circuit like house wiring.
misconceptions.fix: At the synapse, the electrical signal is converted into a chemical signal (neurotransmitter) to cross the gap.

probe.question: How does a signal cross the gap between two neurons?
probe.wrong_answer: It jumps across as an electric current.

misconceptions.root_belief: biological systems work exactly like man-made machines
misconceptions.source_hint: HBCSE diagnostic studies on nervous system

misconceptions.statement: The brain is directly involved in the immediate execution of a reflex action.
misconceptions.why: The brain is commonly taught as the 'control center' for all body actions.
misconceptions.fix: Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord for quick responses, though information is sent to the brain later.

probe.question: Which part of the nervous system primarily processes the quick withdrawal of a hand from a hot object?

misconceptions.root_belief: one central controller manages every single action

misconceptions.statement: Plants have a nervous system similar to animals to sense touch.
misconceptions.why: Students observe fast movements in plants like Mimosa and assume the mechanism must be the same as in animals.
misconceptions.fix: Plants use electrochemical means and changes in water amount (turgor pressure) in cells, not specialized nerve cells.

probe.question: How does the 'touch-me-not' plant move its leaves so quickly?
probe.wrong_answer: It uses a network of nerves to send signals.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar behaviors imply identical internal mechanisms
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Light destroys auxin, which is why the plant bends.
misconceptions.why: Students know auxin is absent on the sunny side and assume it was destroyed by light.
misconceptions.fix: Auxin diffuses away from the light towards the shady side of the shoot.

probe.question: What happens to auxin when light falls on one side of a shoot?
probe.wrong_answer: The light burns or destroys the auxin on that side.

misconceptions.root_belief: disappearance is always caused by destruction

misconceptions.statement: Hormones only affect the specific organ they are produced in.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the site of production with the site of action.
misconceptions.fix: Hormones are secreted into the blood and travel to distant target organs to exert their effect.

probe.question: How does adrenaline reach the heart if it is made in the adrenal glands?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays in the gland and sends a signal.

misconceptions.root_belief: action must happen where the cause is located

misconceptions.statement: Feedback mechanism means the body asks the brain for permission to stop a hormone.
misconceptions.why: The everyday use of 'feedback' implies a conscious report or opinion.
misconceptions.fix: Feedback is an automatic process where the level of a substance (like sugar) itself triggers the start or stop of hormone secretion.

probe.question: How does the pancreas know when to stop producing insulin?
probe.wrong_answer: The brain sends a message saying there is enough insulin.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Information can travel in both directions along a single neuron.
misconceptions.why: Students compare neurons to two-way streets or simple wires.
misconceptions.fix: Nerve impulses travel only in one direction: from dendrite to cell body to axon.

probe.question: Can a single nerve fiber carry a signal back from the axon to the dendrite?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, signals can flow both ways.

misconceptions.root_belief: conduits always allow flow in both directions

misconceptions.statement: The cerebellum is the part of the brain used for thinking and memory.
misconceptions.why: Students often use 'brain' and 'cerebrum' or 'cerebellum' interchangeably without distinguishing functions.
misconceptions.fix: The cerebrum is for thinking and memory; the cerebellum maintains posture and balance.

probe.question: Which part of the brain helps you remember a poem?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding names have the same function

misconceptions.statement: All plant hormones are meant to increase growth.
misconceptions.why: The word 'hormone' is associated with growth and 'boosters' in popular culture.
misconceptions.fix: Some hormones, like Abscisic acid, act as growth inhibitors and cause wilting of leaves.

probe.question: What is the function of Abscisic acid in plants?
probe.wrong_answer: It helps the plant grow taller.

misconceptions.root_belief: biological regulators only act as activators

misconceptions.statement: Involuntary actions like heartbeat are controlled by our will if we concentrate.
misconceptions.why: Students believe the mind has total control over the body.
misconceptions.fix: Involuntary actions are controlled by the midbrain and hindbrain (medulla) and cannot be consciously controlled.

probe.question: Can you stop your heartbeat by thinking about it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if I concentrate hard enough.

misconceptions.root_belief: the conscious mind controls all bodily processes

misconceptions.statement: Plants move towards light because they 'want' to get more food.
misconceptions.why: Students assign human-like intentions and desires to plants.
misconceptions.fix: Plant movement is a mechanical growth response triggered by chemical gradients (auxin), not a conscious choice.

probe.question: Why does a plant stem bend towards a window?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it knows the light is there and wants to reach it.

misconceptions.root_belief: all living things act with conscious intent
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Adrenaline only speeds up the heart and has no other effects.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the most visible or felt symptom of an adrenaline rush.
misconceptions.fix: Adrenaline affects multiple targets: it increases heart rate, diverts blood to muscles, and increases breathing rate.

probe.question: What happens to the digestive system during a 'fight or flight' response?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, only the heart is affected.

misconceptions.root_belief: one hormone has only one specific effect
